Question: Are mathematics students at HYPSM able to prove anything asked on abstract algebra exams without looking into textbooks and/or memorizing known proofs? Is too hard for any student to do proofs out of their own heads under time pressure?
Answer: Such questions get asked quite regularly, and they reveal some common misunderstandings. Math students generally won’t be able to answer anything asked on a test for a course they haven’t taken yet. If it’s a course they did take then yes, many serious students of math could do well on a test for a course they just took and sometimes, but not always, for a course they took last semester or last year. “Memorizing proofs” is a strange myth. It’s really not a thing. Proofs you understand you don’t need to memorize – in fact you can’t memorize. “Memorizing” is just not the right term to describe proofs you’ve internalized. I know many proofs, and I won’t describe any of them as something I’ve “memorized”. On the other hand, if you somehow commit full proofs to memory, you won’t do well on the exam. You won’t be able to apply your understanding to any new problem you haven’t seen before. Even if an exam question asks to present the proof of a known theorem, it takes two sentences to see if a student is writing up a reasoned argument they understand or regurgitating some textbook proof, verbatim. Now, sometimes there’s a key trick or approach that may not be obvious and you may need to remember. That’s fine. It’s not “memorizing a proof”, it’s recalling an idea. There’s another related myth, and that is that exam problems are about specific things you’ve learned. They are not. A final exam looks to see if students are able to apply their understanding to questions they’ve never seen before. That’s the whole point. Consequently, the exam questions (which sometimes show up) that ask to prove a specific theorem studied in class are the easiest questions on the exam. They are considered a giveaway. All of the above is true A) regardless of the course, be it abstract algebra or complex variables or measure theory, and B) regardless of whether the school is “HYPSM” (an acronym I had to look up) or the University of Milan or Warwick or Ohio State. Good students retain their knowledge and are able to apply their understanding throughout their undergrad years and beyond. Students who struggle with the material may not be able to do so, and it doesn’t matter if they are at Harvard or a small community college. To the second question, “Is it too hard for any students to do proofs out of their own heads under time pressure” – like everything else, it’s hard for some students and not very challenging for others. It’s not “too hard” for everyone. If you’re asking these questions because you’re struggling with your current abstract algebra class, I’m sorry. The path forward isn’t to wonder how come anyone is able to do that, and “HYPSM” isn’t some magical place with magical beings. Work through the material, do the problem sets yourself, read the textbook, write up your own version of a proof in your own words, work with fellow students, and use the office hours for advice and guidance. Don’t worry about how or why some other people may or may not be able to do it. (…)

Question: Can a natural logarithmic function be drawn or graph it with its complex numbers in it?
Answer: I think that by “with its complex numbers in it” you mean that you’re looking for a visual representation of the complex function f : C → C , f ( z ) = ln ( z ) . We do have various standard ways of representing complex functions of a complex variable. One of the common ones is to treat the input variable z as a point in the plane, in the usual way: we represent z = x + i y as the point ( x , y ) with cartesian coordinates x and y . On the other hand, the output w = f ( z ) of the function is represented differently: we use brightness to capture the absolute value | w | , and color to represent the argument Arg ( w ) . Therefore, we color each point z in the plane in a way that represents the absolute value and argument of w = f ( z ) . When we do this for w = ln ( z ) we see something like that: To be precise, this is what’s called the principal branch of the logarithm. A few things are nicely visible here: the fact that ln ( 1 ) = 0 is represented by the black dot at z = 1 . The branch cut at the negative real numbers is seen by the mismatching colors (green and blue) right above and below the left part of the x axis: the argument of w = ln ( z ) is close to + π in the northwest, and to − π in the southwest. This is inevitable, and profoundly important in the theory of complex functions. At z = 0 , the logarithm is not defined. You should imagine a “missing point” right at the origin of this diagram. The absolute value | ln ( z ) | is very high near z = 0 , and this is a limitation of this representation method: we can only make the pixels have full “brightness” (value), but we can’t make them shine like a thousand suns. You’ll just have to imagine that ln ( z ) has those extreme value in the vicinity of z = 0 . (…)
